name: Central Square Foundation (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: all CSF's work is in India.
summary: Central Square Foundation (CSF) supports Indian state governments' school reforms: the foundational literacy and numeracy missions of 11 states, new pre-primary classes, adaptive-learning software and other EdTech, school report cards for parents, and a pilot for high-potential students. We count its spending in the year to March 2026 against a year of those programmes' learning gains, credited by CSF's share of everyone's resources behind them (about 3% for the state missions, the largest branch) and valued as later earnings. At the defaults it comes to about 0.85 years of healthy life per $1,000, but the result is mostly uncertainty: how large the missions' learning gain is, how much of a test-score gain lasts into adult earnings, and the discount rate, since the earnings start a decade or more later. Every branch is discounted for missing data except adaptive learning in Andhra Pradesh, which has a randomised trial of the same software in the state's schools.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Students in the government schools of the 11 FLN states
rows.formula: fln_enrolled_as + fln_enrolled_br + fln_enrolled_gj + fln_enrolled_hr + fln_enrolled_mp + fln_enrolled_mh + fln_enrolled_od + fln_enrolled_pb + fln_enrolled_tn + fln_enrolled_ts + fln_enrolled_up
rows.explainer: The 11 states' counts summed (about 2.6 crore); the annual report's total across all 16 states and territories is about 2.85 crore.

rows.label: School grades the enrolment counts span
rows.explainer: Our judgment: most counts are UDISE+ enrolment in schools with Grades 1-5 (Punjab's and Tamil Nadu's are the FLN grades only); the FLN missions target Balvatika to Grade 3. Dividing by 4 (3 to 5) gives the children in one grade: each year one such cohort completes the foundational grades with the missions' gain.

rows.label: Children a year completing the foundational grades in the 11 states
rows.explainer: One cohort a year: a child's three or four years in the FLN grades produce one gain at the end of Grade 3, so a year of the missions is credited with one cohort's gain.

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per standard deviation of skill held in adult life (share of earnings)
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure for low- and middle-income countries: 20% (10% to 30%), from the Center for Global Development's review of studies linking adults' tests to their earnings.

rows.label: Share of an end-of-programme test-score gain still there as skill in adult life
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure: 40% (20% to 70%). Test gains fade after a programme ends; this is the share that lasts into working life.

rows.label: Household sharing multiplier on an earnings gain
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure: an earnings gain is shared within the household.

rows.label: Years an earnings gain lasts, discounted
rows.explainer: A working life (the site's shared 40 years), discounted at the shared rate from when work starts.

rows.label: Units of value per unit of ln(earnings) gained for a working life, at the start of work
rows.explainer: Valued as later income on the site's scale ($uov_per_ln_consumption), like every model of childhood gains that pay off in adult earnings.

rows.label: Learning gain from the state FLN missions per child at the end of Grade 3 (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Our judgment of the missions' causal gain, net of trends and the post-pandemic recovery. Anchors: between 2022 and 2024 Std III reading in rural government schools, where the missions run, rose 7.1 percentage points (to 23.4%) against 2.4 in private schools, and arithmetic 7.4 against 4.4, 'substantially more than recovery' (ASER 2024 all-India presentation, slide 11, https://asercentre.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/ASER-2024-All-India-ppt-Jan-27-11am.pdf): the government schools' extra 3-5 points is about 0.1-0.17 SD on a normal scale; Uttar Pradesh, where CSF has worked since 2019, gained 15.6 points in reading and 20.6 in arithmetic since 2018 (annual report p. 30); structured pedagogy, the missions' model, is among the Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel's 'great buys' (2023 Smart Buys report). ASER's phrase 'substantially more than recovery' is for arithmetic; and between 2022 and 2024 fewer underage children were enrolled in Std I and government schools' share of enrolment fell, either of which can move the gap between government and private schools: reasons for the low end. Government-run missions at state scale get less than trials do. 0.12 SD (0.04 to 0.25).

rows.label: Years from the end of Grade 3 to working age
rows.explainer: Children finish Grade 3 at about 8 and start earning at about 20 (later with more schooling, earlier in rural work): 12 years, from 10 to 14; the earnings gain starts after this wait, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Value of the FLN gain per child (units of value)
rows.explainer: The lasting share of the gain × earnings per SD, as ln(earnings), valued for a working life after the wait.

rows.label: FLN: value of a year's cohort gain in the 11 states, before adjustments
rows.explainer: One year's flow against one year's cost: the states' missions run every year, and CSF's support with them.

rows.label: Children who got pre-primary education for the first time in the reforms CSF supports

source.title: Central Square Foundation, Annual Report 2025-26, 'Learning to Build Tomorrow'
source.quote: ~4 lakh students received access to pre-primary education for the first time ever

rows.explainer: Balvatikas in Uttar Pradesh's government schools, Odisha's Sishu Vatika (about 3.2 lakh enrolled) and Telangana's 1,362 pilot schools (about 18,000), each with CSF's technical support (pp. 35-37). A year's enrolment against a year's support.

rows.label: Learning gain from a year of school-based pre-primary education (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. CSF's dipstick study of 134 Uttar Pradesh Balvatikas found children with a dedicated educator 13-17 points ahead on most tasks (pp. 35-36), but without random assignment; reviews of pre-primary programmes in low- and middle-income countries find school-readiness gains of roughly 0.1 to 0.3 SD, smaller where children would otherwise attend an anganwadi, as many here would. 0.15 SD (0.05 to 0.3).

rows.label: Years from pre-primary to working age
rows.explainer: Children in pre-primary are about 5-6 years old and start earning at about 20 (later with more schooling, earlier in rural work): 14 years, from 12 to 16, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Early childhood: value of a year's enrolment, before adjustments
rows.formula: ece_units_affected_per_year * ln(1 + ece_gain_sd * learning_persistence * earnings_gain_per_sd) * lnc_value_per_unit_gain * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -ece_years_to_work
rows.explainer: Children × the lasting gain valued as later earnings, as in the FLN branch.

rows.label: Learning gain from a year of personalised adaptive learning in government schools (standard deviations)

source.title: Central Square Foundation, 'PAL Works' brochure (28 January 2026), Study 1: randomised trial in Andhra Pradesh by the University of Chicago's Development Innovation Lab
source.quote: In just 17 months, students in PAL-enabled classrooms improved 2.5x times (0.43 SD) compared to those in non-PAL classrooms.

rows.explainer: The Andhra Pradesh trial of the same software (SwiftPAL) in the state's own deployment, 14,000 students in Grades 6-9, maths: 0.74 SD against 0.31 SD in control schools over 17 months, 0.43 SD more, about 0.3 SD a year (0.43 × 12 ÷ 17). Range: 0.15 (Rajasthan's government-school trial of Mindspark, 0.22 SD in maths over 18 months, same brochure p. 4) to 0.4; only maths was measured, and use at scale is 80 minutes a week.

rows.explainer: The Andhra Pradesh trial's gain taken for Himachal Pradesh's PM SHRI schools, thin (its missing-data row).

rows.label: Learners benefiting from the EdTech accelerator's product improvements, 2023 to 2025

source.title: Central Square Foundation, Annual Report 2025-26, 'Learning to Build Tomorrow'
source.quote: Between 2023 and 2025, the LiftEd EdTech Accelerator worked with eight organisations and reached over 55 lakh users, including more than 30 lakh learners who directly benefited from accelerator-driven innovations

rows.explainer: The accelerator's 30 lakh learners over its three years. EdTech Tulna's product reviews (56 lakh students in states' procurement) and AI Samarth's AI-literacy lessons (25 lakh learners) reach many of the same children with no measured learning effect; the small judged gain below covers them too.

rows.label: Years the accelerator's learner count covers
rows.explainer: 'Between 2023 and 2025' (p. 39): three years, or two if the count is from the start of 2023 to the start of 2025.

rows.label: Learners a year benefiting from the accelerator's product improvements
rows.explainer: The three years' count as a yearly flow.

rows.label: Learning gain per learner from better EdTech products and procurement (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the accelerator's quasi-experimental study (released April 2026) found positive effects of at-home EdTech on foundational learning (p. 40) but no figure is published; most of the gain is the products' own, and at-home use is light (Chimple in Ghaziabad: 62% of students active, 30-35 minutes a week, p. 41). CSF's part is the improvement over the products as they were. 0.01 SD (0.002 to 0.04).

rows.label: Other EdTech: value of a year's improvements, before adjustments
rows.formula: edo_units_affected_per_year * ln(1 + edo_gain_sd * learning_persistence * earnings_gain_per_sd) * lnc_value_per_unit_gain * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -fln_years_to_work
rows.explainer: Mostly primary-grade learners, so the FLN branch's wait to working age.

rows.label: Students in schools whose learning reports now go to parents (Jodhpur and Angul districts)

source.title: Central Square Foundation, Annual Report 2025-26, 'Learning to Build Tomorrow'
source.quote: ~1 lakh students covered by first-time competency-based assessments

rows.explainer: Jodhpur's 1,339 schools (about 70,000 students in Grades 6-9) and Angul's 1,362 schools (about 30,000 in Grades 5 and 8), where school-level report cards went to parents for the first time with CSF's support (pp. 44-45). Accreditation frameworks and state school standards authorities in six states have reached no parent yet: their effect would come through the same disclosure once it happens, and is not counted.

rows.label: Learning gain per child from school report cards for parents, a lasting one-time rise (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Report cards on every school in Pakistani villages raised test scores by about 0.11 SD, mostly through competition between private schools (Andrabi, Das and Khwaja, American Economic Review 2017), a rise in the level of learning that lasted, so credited once per child; government schools with no rival nearby respond less, and a large school-quality programme in Madhya Pradesh had no effect on learning (Muralidharan and Singh 2020). 0.04 SD (0 to 0.11).

rows.label: Years from Grades 5-9 to working age
rows.explainer: Students in Grades 5-9 are about 10-15 years old (12 on average) and start earning at about 20 (later with more schooling, earlier in rural work): 8 years, from 6 to 10, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Years a student is in the grades whose report cards go to parents
rows.explainer: Jodhpur's disclosure covers Grades 6-9 (four years) and Angul's assessment Grades 5 and 8; a child moves through about three such years. The report cards' gain is a rise in the level of learning that lasts (Andrabi, Das and Khwaja), so it is credited once per child, not each year the child is covered. 3 (2 to 4).

rows.label: School governance: value of the gain per child (units of value)
rows.explainer: The lasting gain valued as later earnings.

rows.label: Chance each disclosure pilot becomes lasting district practice
rows.explainer: Our judgment: Jodhpur expanded from 54 schools to the whole district and Odisha approved public disclosure of school reports, with a second pilot in about 700 schools (p. 45); but both rest on district collectors who move on, and NEP 2020's call for public disclosure has been slow to take hold. 50% (20% to 80%).

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer for how many years a won reform counts (Your values → How impact is counted; docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Years from the decision to the first report cards reaching parents
rows.explainer: Jodhpur's reports went to parents between September 2025 and March 2026 (p. 44); half a year, from 0 to 1.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
School governance: value of the disclosure reforms, before adjustments
rows.explainer: New students a year (students ÷ the years each is covered) × the value of the gain per student × the chance the practice lasts × the discounted years a won reform counts. The reform's running costs (district staff's and teachers' time on the assessments and report cards) count in CSF's share of the resources and in the side effects' teacher-time harm, not again here.

source.quote: Year 1 Pilot: 5 Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas (JNVs), ~400 students

rows.explainer: Our judgment: the pilot reports 'measurable gains in scientific reasoning, mathematical problem-solving and communication' (p. 47) from five partners' treatment and control groups, no effect size published; enrichment for already selective residential schools. 0.1 SD (0 to 0.3).

Evidence adjustment: publication bias and the conversion to standard deviations
rows.explainer: One question no other row asks: education trials with large effects are more often published, which inflates the trial evidence behind the judged gains (pre-primary, report cards, software), and ASER's threshold shares become standard deviations only on an assumed normal scale. How the states' tests or rich-country wage data fit is in each gain's and the shared earnings figure's own range, and not being measured for CSF is the missing-data step. Our judgment, 0.85 (0.65 to 1).

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have come without CSF's support rather than another partner's
rows.explainer: For the branches where CSF supports a state programme (FLN, early childhood, adaptive learning) or other organisations' products (other EdTech): the programmes would run without CSF, and their gain is credited to CSF only by its share of the resources. This row asks whether another technical partner (Language and Learning Foundation, Pratham, consulting firms, other funders of EdTech) would have filled CSF's role, as several already work alongside it (Haryana: p. 20). Our judgment, 85% (60% to 100%).

rows.label: School governance: share that wouldn't have come without CSF rather than another partner
rows.explainer: CSF designed and ran the Jodhpur and Angul disclosure pilots with the districts (pp. 44-45); no other partner was doing this there. 95% (80% to 100%).

rows.label: High-potential students: share that wouldn't have come without CSF rather than another partner
rows.explainer: CSF set up and funded the STEM accelerator itself (p. 47). 95% (80% to 100%).

rows.label: Central government budget for the NIPUN Bharat mission, a year (₹)

source.title: Careers360, 'Centre has spent under 55% of budgets for Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan, mid-day meal scheme this year' (report on the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, 25 March 2026)
source.quote: It also wants the government to increase budget allocation to Rs 6,000 crore from Rs 2,500 crore.

rows.explainer: The mission's central allocation, ₹2,500 crore a year, as the article on the standing committee's report gives it (the sentence is about the NIPUN Bharat mission, which the committee says 'is set to be wound up this financial Year'). Spending is the next rows.

rows.label: Centre's share of the mission's spending (the rest is the states')
rows.explainer: Samagra Shiksha, through which the mission is funded, is shared 60:40 between the centre and most states and 90:10 for the north-eastern and Himalayan states (Assam among CSF's 11): 62% (60% to 70%) for CSF's states.

rows.label: Children enrolled in Grades 1-5 in India, all schools, 2024-25

source.title: UDISE+ 2024-25 national summary (Ministry of Education data), compiled by Education for All in India

rows.explainer: All schools, government and private.

rows.label: Grades in India's primary stage

source.title: Unacademy, 'School enrolment trends: UDISE+ 2024-25' (29 August 2025)

rows.explainer: UDISE+ counts primary enrolment over Classes 1 to 5.

rows.label: Government schools' share of Grade 1-5 enrolment
rows.explainer: Our judgment: government schools (central and state, not government-aided) enrol 12.16 crore of the 23.29 crore children in Grades 1-12 in 2024-25 (UDISE+), 52%, and a larger share in the primary grades than in secondary. 55% (48% to 62%).

rows.label: CSF's 11 FLN states' share of India's government primary-school children, per grade
rows.explainer: One grade's worth of children in the 11 states over one grade's worth in government primary schools nationally (Grades 1-5, so five grades).

rows.label: Other partners' yearly spending on FLN support in the same states (₹)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: other non-profits and funders work on the same missions (Language and Learning Foundation and Sampark in Haryana, Leadership For Equity, Pratham, Room to Read, Madhi Foundation; pp. 20, 23, 33), several on CSF's scale. ₹300 crore (₹150 to ₹600 crore) a year.

rows.label: Share of the mission's central allocation actually spent
rows.explainer: The ₹2,500 crore is an allocation. Samagra Shiksha, the scheme that funds the mission, had spent 54.9% of its 2025-26 budget estimate by the committee's report (same article), with the year's last weeks to come. 80% (55% to 100%).

rows.label: CSF's own yearly spending on FLN, with its share of overhead (₹)
rows.explainer: FLN's share of all CSF's spending.

rows.label: FLN: CSF's share of the resources behind the missions' gain
rows.formula: fln_csf_inr / (fln_csf_inr + nipun_central_inr * nipun_utilisation / central_share_nipun * csf_states_enrolment_share + fln_other_partners_inr)
rows.explainer: CSF's FLN spending over everyone's: the mission's central budget, as spent, grossed up by the states' share and taken for CSF's 11 states, plus other partners'. Teachers' regular pay isn't counted: they were teaching anyway, and the gain is measured against schooling as usual.

rows.label: States' yearly spending on the new pre-primary classes CSF supports (₹)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: over 5,000 educators deployed in Uttar Pradesh alone (about ₹60 crore a year at contract pay), materials for 70,000 Balvatikas and 45,000 Sishu Vatikas, educators and helpers in Telangana's 1,362 schools (pp. 35-37). ₹300 crore (₹200 to ₹400 crore).

rows.label: Share of the states' pre-primary spending that serves the first-time children counted
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the benefit counts only the ~4 lakh children with pre-primary for the first time (p. 34); the states' spending also serves children who had some pre-primary before, mostly in anganwadis, whose smaller gain isn't counted. CSF's support is aimed at the new classes. 60% (40% to 80%).

rows.label: Early childhood: CSF's share of the resources behind the new pre-primary classes
rows.explainer: CSF's early-childhood spending, with its share of overhead, over its own and the states' spending on the first-time children.

rows.label: Share of CSF's EdTech spending on the states' adaptive-learning deployments
rows.explainer: Our judgment: technical support units in Andhra Pradesh and Himachal Pradesh, against the accelerator, product reviews, AI literacy, the evidence studies and the units in Odisha and Uttar Pradesh (pp. 39-41). 25% (15% to 40%).

rows.label: States' and researchers' yearly spending behind the adaptive-learning deployments (₹)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: about 4.3 lakh students' software licences, devices and teachers' 80 minutes a week of class time in 1,500-plus schools (Andhra Pradesh is fully state-funded: brochure p. 3), and the University of Chicago team's trial. ₹100 crore (₹60 to ₹200 crore).

rows.label: Adaptive learning in Himachal Pradesh: CSF's share of the resources
rows.explainer: The same share as Andhra Pradesh's: the deployments' costs and CSF's support are counted together.

rows.label: Adaptive learning: CSF's share of the resources behind the state deployments
rows.formula: total_expenses_inr * edtech_spend_share * pal_share_of_edtech / (total_expenses_inr * edtech_spend_share * pal_share_of_edtech + pal_state_inr)
rows.explainer: CSF's spending on the deployments, with its share of overhead, over its own and the others'.

rows.label: Partner organisations' yearly spending on the products the accelerator improves (₹)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: Sesame Workshop India, ThinkZone, Top Parent, Chimple and the accelerator's other partners build and run their products with their own funders' money, several on budgets of a few crore to tens of crore a year. ₹40 crore (₹15 to ₹100 crore).

rows.label: Other EdTech: CSF's share of the resources behind the product improvements
rows.formula: total_expenses_inr * edtech_spend_share * (1 - pal_share_of_edtech) / (total_expenses_inr * edtech_spend_share * (1 - pal_share_of_edtech) + edo_partners_inr)
rows.explainer: CSF's other EdTech spending, with its share of overhead, over its own and the partners'.

rows.label: Share of CSF's governance spending on the disclosure pilots
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the Jodhpur and Angul pilots against accreditation frameworks and school standards authorities in six states (pp. 44-45). 40% (20% to 60%).

rows.label: Districts' yearly spending of staff and teachers' time on the assessments and report cards (₹)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: district officials, teachers and parent-teacher meetings in about 2,700 schools for one assessment and report-card round a year (pp. 44-45). ₹3 crore (₹1 to ₹8 crore).

rows.label: School governance: CSF's share of the resources behind the disclosure reforms
rows.formula: total_expenses_inr * gov_spend_share * gov_disclosure_share / (total_expenses_inr * gov_spend_share * gov_disclosure_share + gov_district_inr)
rows.explainer: CSF's spending on the pilots, with its share of overhead, over its own and the districts'.

rows.label: Share of CSF's high-potential students spending on the STEM pilot
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the accelerator's first year against the new Delhi and Telangana partnerships, the Altius programme and two publications (pp. 47-48). 50% (30% to 80%).

rows.label: Partners' and the schools' yearly spending on the STEM pilot (₹)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: five partner organisations' staff and materials and the Navodaya schools' teachers' time for about 400 students. ₹2 crore (₹1 to ₹5 crore).

rows.label: High-potential students: CSF's share of the resources behind the pilot
rows.formula: total_expenses_inr * hps_spend_share * hps_pilot_share / (total_expenses_inr * hps_spend_share * hps_pilot_share + hps_partners_inr)
rows.explainer: CSF's spending on the pilot, with its share of overhead, over its own and the partners'.

rows.label: FLN: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the children are the states' own counts, but the missions' gain is our judgment from national trends, not a controlled evaluation of CSF-supported implementation.

rows.label: Early childhood: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the gain is our judgment from other programmes and an uncontrolled comparison.

rows.label: Adaptive learning in Andhra Pradesh: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Measured: the students are Andhra Pradesh's count and the effect is the randomised trial of the same software in the state's own deployment (pal_gain_sd).

rows.label: Adaptive learning in Himachal Pradesh: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the effect is Andhra Pradesh's trial, taken for another state's deployment.

rows.label: Other EdTech: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no published effect for the improvements.

rows.label: School governance: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the effect is from a different setting (Pakistani villages' private schools).

rows.label: High-potential students: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no published effect size.

CSF's share of the resources, outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.formula: (fln_downstream_value * fln_attribution_share + ece_downstream_value * ece_attribution_share + pal_downstream_value * pal_attribution_share + php_downstream_value * php_attribution_share + edo_downstream_value * edo_attribution_share + gov_downstream_value * gov_attribution_share + hps_downstream_value * hps_attribution_share) / downstream_value
rows.explainer: Each branch's own share applies in its branch; this average is for reading only.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch's own share applies in its branch.

rows.label: Missing-data step, outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.formula: (fln_downstream_value * fln_attribution_share * fln_missing_data_adj + ece_downstream_value * ece_attribution_share * ece_missing_data_adj + pal_downstream_value * pal_attribution_share * pal_missing_data_adj + php_downstream_value * php_attribution_share * php_missing_data_adj + edo_downstream_value * edo_attribution_share * edo_missing_data_adj + gov_downstream_value * gov_attribution_share * gov_missing_data_adj + hps_downstream_value * hps_attribution_share * hps_missing_data_adj) / (fln_downstream_value * fln_attribution_share + ece_downstream_value * ece_attribution_share + pal_downstream_value * pal_attribution_share + php_downstream_value * php_attribution_share + edo_downstream_value * edo_attribution_share + gov_downstream_value * gov_attribution_share + hps_downstream_value * hps_attribution_share)
rows.explainer: Every branch takes the shared missing-data step except Andhra Pradesh's adaptive learning; this average is for reading only.

rows.label: All adjustments combined, outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.formula: (fln_downstream_value * fln_total_adj + ece_downstream_value * ece_total_adj + pal_downstream_value * pal_total_adj + php_downstream_value * php_total_adj + edo_downstream_value * edo_total_adj + gov_downstream_value * gov_total_adj + hps_downstream_value * hps_total_adj) / downstream_value
rows.explainer: For reading only: the outcome below applies each branch's own combined adjustment.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Each effect not modelled, with its sign: better learning keeps children in school longer and goes with later marriage and better health for their own children (+5%, 0 to +15%); civic and non-earnings value of literacy beyond wages (+2%, 0 to +5%); teachers' and mentors' time spent on data entry, assessments and app reporting instead of teaching, and pressure to report inflated results (-2%, -8% to 0). Net +5%, the parts' ranges combined: -5% to +20%.

rows.label: Total value (units of value)
rows.formula: (fln_downstream_value * fln_total_adj + ece_downstream_value * ece_total_adj + pal_downstream_value * pal_total_adj + php_downstream_value * php_total_adj + edo_downstream_value * edo_total_adj + gov_downstream_value * gov_total_adj + hps_downstream_value * hps_total_adj) * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj) + moved_value + careers_value
rows.explainer: Each branch's value × its own adjustments, plus the side effects; money moved and career changes are zero.
